The irreversible anthropogenic perturbation of the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024), manifest in geomorphological transformations (Nixon, 2011), has garnered terminological acknowledgment through the neologism 'Anthropocene' (Moore, 2016), initially proposed by Stoermer and Crutzen in 2000 (Nixon, 2011). Their revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) entails the introduction of the 'Anthropocene epoch', intended to supplant the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), thereby emphasizing the unprecedented biophysical dominance exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This paradigmatic shift in geological thought (Barnosky et al., 2011) seeks to underscore the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's systems, precipitating a new era of anthropogenic influence (Witze, 2024).

The Anthropocene epoch is characterized by a distinct set of geological features, including the widespread presence of anthropogenic sediments (Nixon, 2011), the alteration of natural landscapes (Haraway, 2016), and the emergence of novel biota (Barnosky et al., 2011). This epoch marks a significant departure from the Holocene, which was characterized by a more stable and pristine biophysical environment (Smith & Zeder, 2013). The Anthropocene epoch is thus a testament to the profound and far-reaching consequences of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024).

Furthermore, the concept of the Anthropocene has been subject to various critiques and debates (Haraway, 2016), with some scholars arguing that it oversimplifies the complex relationships between human and natural systems (Barnosky et al., 2011). Nevertheless, the Anthropocene remains a widely accepted and influential concept in the fields of geology, ecology, and environmental studies (Nixon, 2011).

In conclusion, the Anthropocene epoch represents a significant shift in our understanding of the Earth's biophysical systems and the impact of human activities on the environment. This concept has garnered widespread recognition and has sparked important discussions about the future of our planet (Witze, 2024).
